narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3—compared to an average around the 6th decile among accepted students—signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam. These academic performance indicators outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score was the next most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 33, your score is below the 37 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated it as a mild positive signal that slightly increased your chances of passing.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0 (versus 3.23 for accepted students), middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking the LSAT for a higher score, enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program to raise your GPA, or gaining targeted legal experience that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous work. These steps can directly address the factors that led to your rejection. (218 words)
